81911.subject: Binance Traces Its Hack to a Fake Job Interview
81911.body:
**gm, Defiers!**

These are the biggest stories in DeFi and crypto:

* [**Binance**](https://thedefiant.io/news/hacks/binance-details-months-long-campaign-behind-6-34-billion-hack)[ traced its hack to a fake job interview](https://thedefiant.io/news/hacks/binance-details-months-long-campaign-behind-6-34-billion-hack)

* [**The CFTC**](https://thedefiant.io/converge/regulation/cftc-chair-says-equity-perps-can-begin-us-trading)[ cleared single-stock perps; Cboe's group sued](https://thedefiant.io/converge/regulation/cftc-chair-says-equity-perps-can-begin-us-trading)

* [**Kraken**](https://thedefiant.io/news/hacks/kraken-restricts-accounts-amid-suspected-133-million-plus-eu-theft)[ restricted accounts over a $133M theft](https://thedefiant.io/news/hacks/kraken-restricts-accounts-amid-suspected-133-million-plus-eu-theft)

* [**SEC staff**](https://thedefiant.io/news/regulation/sec-staff-grants-canton-coin-no-action-relief-for-token-minting)[ called Canton Coin a digital commodity](https://thedefiant.io/news/regulation/sec-staff-grants-canton-coin-no-action-relief-for-token-minting)

* [**Ethereum**](https://thedefiant.io/news/blockchains/justin-drake-targets-december-2028-for-ethereum-s-post-quantum-transition)[ eyes a post-quantum switch by 2028](https://thedefiant.io/news/blockchains/justin-drake-targets-december-2028-for-ethereum-s-post-quantum-transition)

Binance says the attack that cost it about $6.34 billion started with a job interview. In a [technical report](https://thedefiant.io/news/hacks/binance-details-months-long-campaign-behind-6-34-billion-hack) published today, it said a recruiter on a legitimate job site approached one of its engineers in September. After a first video interview, a person posing as a company CEO told him in a second interview to download a coding assignment onto his work computer. The code [replaced a development-tool component](https://thedefiant.io/news/hacks/fake-job-interview-opened-path-to-6-34-billion-hack-binance-says) and hid from Binance's security software.

The attackers then moved from one engineer to the next. On Oct. 20, they used that computer and an internal AI tool to reach two wallet engineers. On one of their machines, they found a credential that could deploy software. On Oct. 29, they used it to run a script inside Binance's wallet-signing service. That service signed the [EIP-7702 delegation](https://thedefiant.io/news/security/binance-labeled-wallet-swept-minutes-after-eip-7702-delegation) that let an outside contract empty a hot wallet. Co-CEO Richard Teng called it "a months-long campaign."

The report also corrects Binance's first account, which said outflows stopped when it paused withdrawals. The delegation sat onchain, outside the withdrawal system, so the pause did not cancel it. Binance signs with multiparty computation, so no single key could revoke the permission quickly. Its team built a procedure and cleared the delegation at 8:10 p.m. ET on Oct. 29. _— George Orwell, __1984_



----------View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/e617ab51-fd48-407f-a30c-9c4713fe789b/unnamed.jpg?t=1793743779)
Caption: 

# Private keys as easy as 1,2,3

The basic idea of elliptic-curve cryptography is that it's easy to go forward along a mathematically defined curve and effectively impossible to go back. 

What you move forward toward is a public key: a two-dimensional point (x,y) located somewhere along a “curve” defined by a mathematical equation.

(I used scare quotes there because the equation produces a scatterplot of coordinates that only a mathematician could identify as a curve.) 

What gets you there is a private key: Starting from a fixed base point on the curve (G), you add G to itself some number of times (d) to arrive at the public key (x,y).

D is the private key: an integer you plug into the curve’s equation to get to the public key.

The practical result is that deriving a public key from a private key (going forward) takes milliseconds, but deriving a private key from a public key (going backward) would take billions of years. 

I can’t explain exactly why going backward takes as long as that, but I know it has something to do with elliptic curve math.

The important thing is what this makes possible: e-commerce, private messaging, biometric authentication, cryptocurrency.

Elliptic-key cryptography allows two complete strangers to communicate securely over a public network without having agreed on a secret code in advance.

To participate, all you need is a private key that’s long enough that no one will guess it.

Because someone might try.

In crypto, for example, private keys typically look something like: 4f9a2c88e5d1b703e498c116a82705f32b859e4d07c31fae81b6dc24089e9247. 

Despite the letters involved, this is just a number. Each hexadecimal digit in the string (number or letter) represents four bits of binary data (f = 1111, 8 = 1000, e
